3D-Ultraschall setzt viele Schnitte zu e:
3D ultrasound combines many slices into a three-dimensional image; 4D also shows it in motion. The images look like photos and are therefore popular.

## What applies in Germany?

Since 2021, ultrasound on pregnant women may only be done for a medical reason. Offers that only promise nice pictures or videos, so-called “baby TV”, are not allowed. This applies to 2D just as much as to 3D and 4D. The reason: every scan puts sound energy into the tissue, and without a health benefit it should be avoided.

## When does 3D make sense?

In some cases, a 3D image can help, for example for a more detailed assessment of the face, spine or shape of the womb. Your doctor then decides whether it is needed for clarification.

## And the lovely memories?

Many practices will give you a picture from the basic scan if you ask, but there is no obligation to do so. In Babyliebe you’ll find a self-made ultrasound view of the 3D model of your baby for the current week. It is not a medical image and not a real finding; it is only meant to give you an idea.

## If you are worried

An additional ultrasound makes sense if there is a medical reason, such as bleeding or fewer baby movements. In such cases, call your practice or hospital.

Feel free to ask at your check-up what can be seen on the image.

Allergien haben viele Ursachen und lasse:
Allergies have many causes and can’t be reliably prevented. According to the current guideline, there are some recommendations that can lower the risk, and some earlier advice that is now outdated.

## What is recommended

- **Breastfeeding:** breastfeeding is recommended regardless of the allergy risk. According to this guideline, solids should start between the beginning of the 5th and the beginning of the 7th month, ideally while you continue breastfeeding.
- **Smoke-free:** no tobacco smoke during pregnancy or around your child.
- **Vaccinations:** vaccinations should follow the vaccination schedule; they don’t increase the risk of allergies.
- **Mould and damp:** avoid mould in your home and air it regularly.
- **Pets:** cats and dogs don’t have to be given away if there is an allergy risk. If the risk is increased, getting a new cat for the family is rather discouraged.
- **Overweight** in childhood should be avoided if possible.

## Solids and allergens

It used to be recommended to avoid egg, fish or nuts for a long time. That is outdated. Today the advice is: introduce potential allergens such as hen’s egg, peanut (as a smooth paste), fish, wheat and dairy products in the first year of life along with solids. Avoiding them not only doesn’t lower the risk but can increase it. Make sure they are in a safe form, for example well-cooked eggs and nut butter instead of whole nuts.

## If the risk is increased

If a parent or sibling has an allergy or your baby has eczema, the risk is increased. Talk to your paediatrician before introducing peanut, egg or other allergens. They will advise you on how to proceed.

## How do you recognise an allergy?

Typical signs are a skin rash, hives, swelling of the lips or face, vomiting, diarrhoea or difficulty breathing after eating. If there is swelling of the face or difficulty breathing, call 112 immediately. For milder signs, contact your paediatrician.

## What doesn’t help

Special diets during pregnancy or breastfeeding, avoiding allergens for your baby, and hypoallergenic formula when the risk isn’t increased.

Breathing is the simplest help during labour and is always available. It calms the nervous system, provides oxygen and gives the contraction a rhythm. There is no single right technique; you’ll find out what suits you by practising.

## The basis: breathing deep into your belly

Place one hand on your belly. Breathe in through your nose and feel your belly rise. Breathe out slowly through your mouth. The out-breath should be longer than the in-breath, for example four seconds in, six seconds out. This activates relaxation.

## Breathing through contractions

- **At the beginning:** breathe calmly and deeply, keep your shoulders loose. Consciously let go between contractions.
- **With stronger contractions:** breathe out slowly while making a deep sound (for example “ooo” or “aaa”). Making sounds opens and relaxes the jaw, and the jaw is connected to the pelvic floor.
- **During transition:** short, shallow breaths can help if you feel the urge to push before the cervix is fully open.

## Pushing

In the pushing stage, you push the way your body tells you. Your midwife guides you. As the head is born, it helps to pant briefly so that the tissue has time to stretch.

## How to practise

Practise for five to ten minutes every day, together with your partner if you like. Try out positions: on all fours, standing, leaning against a wall, on a birthing ball. An antenatal class goes deeper into this.

## What really counts

You can’t do anything wrong. If your breathing supports you, it is right. If the pain is very strong, you may choose additional help at any time.

There are many abbreviations on the ultrasound image and in the German maternity record (Mutterpass). The most important ones (German abbreviation in brackets where it differs):

- **CRL** (SSL) – crown–rump length. It is measured in the first weeks, while the baby is curled up, and determines the due date.
- **BPD** – biparietal diameter, the width of the head between the temples.
- **HC** (KU) – head circumference.
- **AC** (AU / ATD) – abdominal circumference or abdominal diameter.
- **FL** – femur length, the length of the thigh bone.
- **EFW** (FG) – estimated fetal weight, calculated from the measurements.
- **AF** (FW) – amniotic fluid. It is described as an amount, for example normal, a lot or little.
- **EDD** (ET) – estimated due date.
- **Percentile** – shows where your baby lies compared with other babies of the same week. The 50th percentile is the average. Values between about the 10th and 90th are considered usual.

## How much do the numbers mean?

A single value says little. What matters more is whether your baby keeps to their growth curve. The estimated weight can differ from the birth weight by about 10 to 15 percent. A baby who seems “small” or “big” on ultrasound is therefore not automatically so at birth.

## Questions for your doctor

Ask for an explanation if a value is underlined or abnormal. Write your questions down under “Questions for the appointment”. Abnormal values are often a reason to take a closer look, not a diagnosis.

In the first months, babies have some protection from their mother’s antibodies, but it is limited and only works against some diseases. Vaccinations protect against diseases that can be dangerous for young children. The Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) at the Robert Koch Institute in Germany gives recommendations that are updated regularly.

## The most important vaccinations

- **6-in-1 vaccine:** tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b and hepatitis B. It starts at two months, with further doses at four and eleven months.
- **Pneumococcal:** protects against serious infections such as meningitis and pneumonia, also from two months.
- **Rotavirus:** an oral vaccine against severe vomiting and diarrhoea, from week 6, two or three doses depending on the vaccine.
- **Meningococcal B:** protection against a rare but serious form of meningitis, recommended at two, four and twelve months.
- **Measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox:** from 11 months, second dose at 15 months.
- **RSV:** for newborns and infants in their first RSV season, prophylaxis with an antibody is recommended. Ask at your maternity hospital or your paediatrician.

Since 2026, STIKO no longer recommends the meningococcal C vaccination at 12 months. You’ll find the exact dates in the vaccination calendar in Babyliebe.

## Vaccination reactions

Occasionally there is redness and swelling at the injection site, a mild fever, tiredness or restlessness. These usually subside after one to two days. Serious side effects are very rare. If there is a high fever, persistent crying or unusual behaviour, call the practice.

## Vaccinating with a cold?

A mild infection is usually no obstacle. With a fever above 38.5 degrees or an acute illness, the appointment is postponed. If in doubt, ask.

## Vaccination record

The vaccination record should always be brought to the U check-ups. It documents all vaccinations. Your paediatrician will advise you individually.

With twins, ultrasound scans and checks are more frequent, because risks such as differences in growth, high blood pressure or premature birth occur more often. Your practice or hospital sets the exact dates. This overview gives you a guide.

## First trimester

The ultrasound determines whether there are two placentas and how many amniotic sacs. This is the most important decision for the further plan and is most reliable until about week 14.

## From week 16 for monochorionic twins

About every two weeks, it is checked whether the babies’ growth and amniotic fluid are developing similarly. This allows an unequal distribution of blood between the babies to be detected early.

## From week 20 for dichorionic twins

Checks about every four weeks. These are about growth, amniotic fluid and position.

## Further tests

The cervix is often monitored as well, because a premature birth can show there first. Blood pressure, urine and blood values are also checked more closely.

## What you can watch for yourself

- Is your bump getting noticeably bigger within a few days, or are you short of breath?
- Do you feel contractions or a regular pulling, bleeding or leaking amniotic fluid?
- Do you have severe headaches, vision problems or pain in your upper abdomen?

Get in touch immediately in these cases. In an emergency, call 112.

You can enter the dates of your ultrasound checks in the Babyliebe calendar. You’ll then be reminded in good time.

In an induction of labour, contractions are stimulated by medical means when waiting would mean a higher risk for you or your baby. About one in five births in Germany is induced.

## When can an induction make sense?

- if the estimated due date has been clearly exceeded; it is usually offered from 41+0 to 41+3
- if your waters have broken without contractions starting
- with pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure or gestational diabetes
- if the baby’s growth is delayed or there is too little amniotic fluid
- for other medical reasons after medical advice

Whether and when you have an induction is your decision after advice. You may ask what alternatives there are and what the timetable looks like.

## Methods

- **Membrane sweep:** during an examination, the midwife or doctor gently separates the membranes from the cervix. This can stimulate contractions.
- **Prostaglandins:** a gel, tablet or vaginal insert softens the cervix and can trigger contractions.
- **Balloon catheter:** a small balloon stretches the cervix mechanically.
- **Oxytocin (drip):** the hormone is given through a vein and triggers contractions. The baby is monitored by CTG during this.

Often several methods are used one after the other. An induction can take hours to days.

## What you can expect

Contractions after an induction can start stronger and more intensely than when labour begins naturally. Painkillers and an epidural are available as with any other birth. If the induction doesn’t lead to contractions, a caesarean is also possible if it becomes necessary.

## Home remedies

For many home remedies such as castor oil, acupuncture or walks, there is no reliable evidence that they work. Some are not without risk. Talk to your midwife; she knows gentle options.

Bonding is the emotional relationship between your baby and the people who care for them. It gives a child security from which they can discover the world. It doesn’t happen in a single moment, but in everyday life, through many small experiences.

## What supports bonding

- **Sensitivity:** you notice your baby’s signals, interpret them and respond, usually within a reasonable time. This includes hunger, tiredness, the need for closeness, but also signs of being overwhelmed.
- **Physical contact:** skin to skin after the birth, carrying, cuddling and stroking.
- **Eye contact and talking:** look at your baby, talk and sing to them, mirror their smile.
- **Reliability:** recurring rituals and loving responses give security.

## You don’t have to be perfect

No parent senses every need straight away. What matters is that you try on the whole and make up for mistakes. A child forgives a lot if they usually feel safe and loved.

## Bonding and the bottle, caesarean, premature birth

Bonding doesn’t depend on whether you breastfeed or bottle-feed, or whether your child was born vaginally or by caesarean. Bonding can also develop after a difficult birth or separation in the first days, for example with premature babies. Kangaroo care, meaning skin-to-skin contact, helps a lot.

## When it’s hard

Some parents find it hard to connect at first, for example after a distressing birth, with exhaustion or depression. This is not unusual and is not a sign of a lack of love. Talk to your midwife, doctor or an advice centre. Frühe Hilfen (early support services) offer free and confidential support for families. If you feel very low or have thoughts of harming yourself or your child, seek help immediately: Telefonseelsorge 0800 111 0 111, in an emergency 112.

## Fathers and partners too

Bonds develop with all caregivers. Take over changing, carrying, bathing and soothing; this creates your own closeness. Time with your baby, especially in the first weeks, pays off for a long time.

The German Maternity Protection Act protects you and your baby during pregnancy and after the birth. It applies to employees, trainees, students and pupils.

## The protection periods

- Six weeks before the estimated due date: you may carry on working if you wish.
- Eight weeks after the birth: an absolute ban on employment. Twelve weeks in the case of premature or multiple births or if the child has a disability.

## Protection against dismissal

From the start of the pregnancy until four months after the birth, you generally may not be dismissed. Tell your employer about the pregnancy – you can also do this within two weeks of receiving notice.

## At work

Your employer must check whether your work is safe and adapt it if necessary. Night work, heavy lifting and certain hazardous substances are restricted.

## Money

During the protection periods you receive maternity pay from your health insurer and a top-up from your employer – together usually your average net salary.

## After a miscarriage

Since 1 June 2025, a protection period also applies after a miscarriage: two weeks from week 13, six weeks from week 17 and eight weeks from week 20. You can return to work earlier if you wish.

## How to tell your employer

An informal notice is enough. Your employer may ask for a medical certificate confirming the pregnancy and due date, and must pay for it.

The postnatal period lasts about six to eight weeks. Your body heals, your womb shrinks back, and you get to know each other as a family.

## What’s normal

- Lochia: bleeding that becomes lighter and less over weeks
- Afterpains, especially when breastfeeding
- Heavy sweating and mood swings due to the hormonal changes

## Good for you

- Lying down a lot, especially in the first two weeks
- Limiting visitors, accepting help
- Eating and drinking enough
- Making use of your midwife’s daily visits

## Warning signs

Fever, foul-smelling lochia, suddenly heavier bleeding, pain or redness on the breast or scar: please contact your midwife or doctor straight away.

## How the lochia changes

In the first days it is bright red and heavy, after about a week brownish, later yellowish to whitish. It usually stops after four to six weeks. Use pads rather than tampons.

If the bleeding suddenly becomes so heavy that you need more than one pad an hour, or you feel dizzy, call 112.

## Postnatal check

Six to eight weeks after the birth you have your postnatal check with your gynaecologist. It’s best to book the appointment during the postnatal period. Day by day, the postnatal companion in Babyliebe guides you through the first two weeks.

For many, the second trimester is the best time to travel: the nausea is over and the bump isn’t too big yet.

## Flying

In an uncomplicated pregnancy, flying is usually safe. Many airlines require a medical certificate from week 28 and no longer carry pregnant women from about week 36 – find out beforehand. Drink plenty, get up regularly and wear compression stockings on longer flights.

## Driving

Place the lap belt under your bump over your hip bones and the shoulder belt between your breasts. Plan breaks every one to two hours.

## Destinations

Avoid areas with Zika virus, a malaria risk or poor medical care. Get travel health advice before long-distance trips.

## Always with you

Your maternity record, health insurance card, travel health insurance that covers pregnancy and birth, and the address of a local hospital.

## When you’d better not travel

If you have bleeding, premature contractions, a low-lying placenta or high blood pressure, talk to your doctor first. In the last weeks before your due date, it’s best to stay near your maternity hospital.

For every trip, pack your medication, compression stockings and something to eat on the way. On longer car journeys it helps to get out regularly and walk a few steps; this helps prevent thrombosis.

For travel to countries with compulsory vaccinations or particular diseases, get advice early, because some vaccinations are not given during pregnancy.

Your body has achieved something enormous. It needs time to recover, and that takes longer than six weeks. The womb shrinks back, the pelvic floor recovers, the abdominal muscles find their way back. Impatience doesn’t help.

## The first weeks

In the first days, rest, warmth and care matter most. Gentle pelvic floor exercises, walks and light breathing exercises are possible early on if you feel well. Lifting, carrying and strain should stay limited. Your midwife supports you during this phase with home visits.

## Postnatal recovery class

From about six to eight weeks after the birth, or a little later after a caesarean or complications, you can take part in a postnatal recovery class. It strengthens the pelvic floor and abdominal muscles and protects against bladder weakness and back pain. In Germany you are entitled to it up to nine months after the birth, and health insurance covers the costs. Some classes let you bring your baby.

## When is exercise possible again?

Gentle exercise such as walking and swimming (only once the lochia has stopped) is possible early on. For jogging, jumping and intensive abdominal training, wait until your pelvic floor is stable again and your midwife or doctor agrees, often after three to six months. If you have diastasis recti, the separation of the abdominal muscles, you should have targeted training for it.

## Warning signs

Persistent urine leakage, a feeling of pressure downwards, pain during sex or a clearly visible bulge on your belly when sitting up should be checked by a doctor or physiotherapist.

## Be kind to yourself

Your body has changed, and that’s allowed. Don’t compare yourself with others. Healthy food, as much sleep as possible and exercise in small steps are the best basis.

## Back pain

Warmth, pregnancy yoga, swimming and a nursing pillow when sleeping take the strain off. Lift heavy things by bending your knees and wear flat shoes.

## Heartburn

Eat several small meals, avoid very fatty and spicy food and don’t lie down straight after eating. Raising the head of your bed helps. Some swear by almonds or oats.

## Leg cramps

Stretch your calf by pulling your toes towards you. Magnesium can help – discuss taking it with your doctor.

## Fluid retention

Put your feet up, move a lot and drink enough. Compression stockings can help.

## Constipation

Fibre, plenty of water and exercise. Iron supplements can make constipation worse.

Sudden, severe swelling, headaches or vision problems, on the other hand, are a warning sign – then have it checked by a doctor straight away.

## Haemorrhoids

Pressure in the pelvis and constipation encourage haemorrhoids. Soft stools, sitz baths and cooling help. Only use ointments after asking.

## Sciatica and pelvic pain

Pulling pain down the leg or in the pubic bone is common. Warmth, rest and physiotherapy help, and a pelvic support belt can relieve the strain. Mention the pain at your check-up so you get support.

Write down which complaints occur when and mention them at your check-up. Many can be eased with simple measures, and you don’t just have to put up with them.

The pelvic floor is a layer of muscle at the lower end of the pelvis. It supports the bladder, womb and bowel, helps you hold in urine and stools, and plays an important role in the birth. In pregnancy it is under more strain due to the growing weight of the womb and hormonal loosening.

## Why train it?

A well-trained pelvic floor can help prevent bladder weakness during pregnancy and afterwards and make recovery after the birth easier. Both matter: strengthening and relaxing. A pelvic floor that is too tight can make the birth more difficult.

## How to find it

Imagine you had to stop the flow while passing urine or hold in wind. The muscles you tense are parts of the pelvic floor. Your belly, thighs and bottom stay as relaxed as possible.

## Simple exercises

- **Tense and release:** as you breathe out, gently draw the pelvic floor inwards and upwards, hold for three to five seconds, and let go completely as you breathe in. Repeat ten times.
- **The lift:** imagine your pelvic floor moving up in stages and back down again.
- **Relaxing:** on all fours or sitting cross-legged, consciously let your pelvic floor soften as you breathe out, without pushing.

Practise briefly several times a day, for example while brushing your teeth or at the traffic lights.

## Everyday life

When coughing and sneezing, it helps to tense the pelvic floor lightly just beforehand. Heavy lifting and straining put strain on it. Try to prevent constipation.

## When to get help?

If you have urine leakage that lasts, a feeling of pressure downwards or pain, pelvic floor physiotherapy helps. In Germany, health insurance covers it with a doctor’s prescription. After the birth, a postnatal recovery class helps.

The perineum is the tissue between the vagina and the anus. It is stretched a lot during the birth. Sometimes it tears or is cut. Many women worry about this. That’s understandable, and there is quite a lot you can do.

## Perineal massage

From about week 34 of pregnancy, you can massage your perineum regularly, about three to four times a week for five to ten minutes. With clean hands and a little oil, you gently stretch the tissue. Studies show that in first-time mothers, the massage can somewhat lower the risk of severe tears and episiotomies. Your midwife will show you the technique.

## During the birth

Upright, side-lying or all-fours positions often relieve the perineum more than lying on your back. Warm compresses and a slow birth of the head can protect the tissue. Your midwife can guide your pushing.

## Perineal tears

Perineal tears are classified into four degrees. In first- and second-degree tears only skin and muscle are affected; they are usually stitched and heal well. Severe tears (third and fourth degree) affect the anal sphincter and need special treatment and aftercare.

## Episiotomy

An episiotomy (a cut in the perineum) is no longer done routinely. It may be considered if the baby needs to be born quickly, in a ventouse or forceps delivery, or to avoid an impending severe tear.

## After the birth

Cooling in the first days, sitz baths, changing pads often, gently rinsing after using the toilet and rest all support healing. Painkillers may be taken after consulting your midwife or doctor. If the pain increases, you have a fever or foul-smelling discharge from the wound, contact your midwife or doctor.

## The four phases

During **menstruation**, the body sheds the built-up lining of the womb. In the **follicular phase**, a follicle matures in one ovary, controlled by the hormone FSH. Oestrogen levels rise during this time. At **ovulation**, the mature egg is released from the follicle and taken up by the fallopian tube. In the **luteal phase**, the follicle produces the hormone progesterone, which prepares the lining of the womb for a possible implantation. If fertilisation doesn’t happen, hormone levels drop and the period begins.

## When are you fertile?

After ovulation, the egg can only be fertilised for 12 to 24 hours. Sperm, on the other hand, can survive in the body for up to five days. That’s why the fertile window runs from five days before ovulation to the day of ovulation, so about six days. The chance is highest on the two days before ovulation.

Ovulation usually takes place about 14 days before the next period, not necessarily on day 14 of the cycle. In a long cycle it happens later.

## How you can recognise ovulation

- **Cervical mucus:** around ovulation the mucus becomes clear, stretchy and stringy, similar to raw egg white.
- **Basal temperature:** after ovulation your waking temperature rises by about 0.2 to 0.5 degrees and stays higher until the next period. This only shows ovulation in hindsight.
- **Ovulation tests:** they measure the hormone LH in urine, which rises shortly before ovulation.
- **Body awareness:** some people feel a slight pulling in the lower abdomen (mittelschmerz).

A combination of several signs is the most meaningful. An app that only uses average values can only estimate ovulation.

## When you should seek medical advice

If your cycle is very irregular, your period stops, you have very severe pain or bleeding, or if you want a baby and it hasn’t happened after a year (after six months from age 35), it makes sense to see a gynaecologist.

## Naegele’s rule

280 days – that’s 40 weeks – are added to the first day of your last period. If your cycle is longer or shorter than 28 days, the difference is added or subtracted. Babyliebe does this automatically when you enter your cycle length.

## Why the date can change

At the first ultrasound scan, your doctor measures your baby’s crown–rump length. If it differs significantly from the calculation, the date is adjusted. This measurement between weeks 8 and 12 is considered particularly accurate.

## Only a guide

Only about four percent of babies arrive exactly on their estimated due date. A birth between 37+0 and 41+6 is considered normal. You can change the date in Babyliebe at any time – all weeks and content adjust.

## If you don’t know your cycle

If you don’t know the exact first day of your last period, for example after stopping the pill or while breastfeeding, your doctor determines the date from the first ultrasound. After fertility treatment, it is calculated from the day of fertilisation or embryo transfer.

## Early signs

- Lightening contractions: the bump drops and breathing becomes easier.
- Loss of the mucus plug, sometimes slightly bloody. The birth can still be days away.
- Restlessness, nesting instinct, loose stools.
- Practice contractions: the belly becomes hard, but the contractions stay irregular and don’t get stronger.

## Real contractions

Labour contractions become more regular, stronger and longer and don’t go away when you rest or in a warm bath. Many feel them in their back at first; later they move to the front. The contraction timer in Babyliebe shows you the interval and length.

A guide for first-time mothers: contractions every five minutes, each lasting about one minute, for an hour (the 5-1-1 rule). This is a common rule of thumb, not a fixed requirement. Then it’s time to call the hospital or your midwife. If you already have children, have a long journey or had a quick birth before, get in touch earlier. If your hospital has told you something different, follow that.

## Waters breaking

If amniotic fluid is leaking, call the hospital and say what it looks like: clear, greenish or bloody. If the baby’s head isn’t yet firmly in the pelvis or the fluid is greenish, have yourself transported lying down or call an ambulance.

## Call 112 or the hospital immediately

- Heavy bleeding, more than a little bloody mucus
- Green or bloody amniotic fluid
- Constant abdominal pain without a break between contractions
- Noticeably fewer or no baby movements
- Fever
- After your waters break, you feel or see something in the vagina, such as the umbilical cord: call 112 immediately and get onto all fours with your bottom up.

## Before week 37

Regular contractions, a pulling in the back like during a period, pressure downwards or waters breaking before week 37 can signal a premature birth. Then call the hospital immediately.

## Time at home

As long as everything is calm, you can often spend the early phase at home: take a warm shower, eat lightly, drink, move around and rest between contractions. Have your maternity record and hospital bag ready.

## How often

- Up to week 32: every four weeks
- From week 32: every two weeks
- After the estimated due date: usually every two days

## What is checked every time

Weight, blood pressure, urine for protein and sugar, growth of the womb, your baby’s heartbeat and later their position. Everything is recorded in your maternity record (Mutterpass).

## The three routine ultrasound scans

- Weeks 9 to 12
- Weeks 19 to 22
- Weeks 29 to 32

## Further tests

Blood group and antibodies, rubella immunity, HIV test (optional), test for chlamydia, hepatitis B from week 32 and the glucose test between weeks 24 and 28. Additional offers such as extra ultrasound scans that you pay for yourself are optional.

Add your appointments to the Babyliebe calendar – you’ll be reminded in good time.

You can have your antenatal care with a midwife, at the practice or alternating between the two. The ultrasound scans are always done by the doctor.

Bring your maternity record and your questions to every appointment. It’s best to write your questions down between appointments, as it’s easy to forget something during the conversation. Babyliebe has the “Questions for the appointment” tool for this.

## Your baby has its own rhythm

There is no fixed number that applies to everyone. What matters is your baby’s pattern: when is it active, and what do the movements feel like? Many babies are more active in the evening when you settle down. Long sleep phases during the day are normal.

## Movements don’t decrease towards the end

With little room in the womb, kicks turn more into rolling, pushing and stretching. But the number of movements should not decrease until the birth. The idea that babies become quieter shortly before birth is a myth. Fewer movements are a reason to call then too.

## How to pay attention to the movements

From the third trimester, it helps to focus on your baby consciously once a day, ideally at a time when your baby is usually lively. Lie on your side and give yourself some quiet time. There is no fixed number above which everything is fine. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) advises not to rely on fixed counts but on changes: if movements are fewer, weaker or different from usual, that’s what counts. The kick counter in Babyliebe shows you your baby’s pattern over the days.

## When you should act

If you feel noticeably fewer movements than usual or none at all, don’t wait until the next day. Call your hospital or midwife, even at night. Cold drinks or something sweet to “stimulate” the baby don’t replace a check. If you’re unsure whether there are fewer movements, that alone is reason enough to call.

## What happens at the hospital

Usually the heartbeat is recorded with a CTG, often followed by an ultrasound scan. In the vast majority of cases everything is fine and you go home reassured. If it happens again, call again. Every new change deserves a new check.

## No heartbeat monitors at home

Devices or apps for listening to the heartbeat at home don’t replace a check. A heartbeat can often be heard even when the baby isn’t doing well, and can falsely reassure you. The professional society therefore advises against them.

## How do you recognise teething?

Typical signs are more drooling, chewing on objects, restlessness, red and slightly swollen gums and sometimes sore patches on the chin. A slightly raised temperature is possible. High fever and diarrhoea are not part of teething and should be checked.

## What helps?

- cool, but not frozen, teething rings
- a clean, damp, cold cloth to chew on
- massaging the gums with a clean finger
- attention and distraction
- if needed, pain-relieving teething gels after asking at the pharmacy

Amber necklaces are not recommended: they are a choking and injury risk and don’t work.

## Dental care from the start

From the first tooth, brush twice a day with a rice-grain-sized amount of fluoride children’s toothpaste (1000 ppm fluoride), and from the second birthday with a pea-sized amount. Until school age, adults brush again afterwards. Have your paediatrician explain how this fits with the fluoride in the vitamin D supplement so that your child doesn’t get too much fluoride.

## Preventing tooth decay

- no sweetened drinks and no tea in the bottle
- no constant sucking on a bottle or cup
- don’t dip dummies in honey or sugar and don’t lick them
- visit the dentist from the first tooth, twice a year

## When to see a doctor?

If teeth are badly discoloured, there is pain or teeth become loose after a fall.

## What happens in your body

The levels of the pregnancy hormones hCG, progesterone and oestrogen rise sharply. This explains a lot: tiredness, nausea, tender breasts, needing to pass urine more often, a heightened sense of smell and mood swings. Your womb is growing, but your bump usually can’t be seen yet.

## Nausea

Around 70 in 100 pregnant women experience nausea, usually between weeks 6 and 12. It helps to spread small meals over the day, eat something dry before getting up, drink enough in small sips and avoid strong smells. Ginger helps some. If you can hardly keep anything down, are losing weight or feel dizzy, please talk to your doctor.

## Tiredness

It is normal and caused by hormones. Allow yourself rest breaks and go to bed earlier. If possible, lighten your load in everyday life.

## Important appointments

Make an appointment with your gynaecologist early. There the pregnancy is confirmed, your maternity record is created and blood values are measured. The first ultrasound scan takes place between weeks 9 and 12. At antenatal appointments, your vaccination status, medication and pre-existing conditions are discussed.

## What you can keep in mind now

Take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily until the end of week 12. Avoid alcohol and smoking, avoid raw foods with a risk of listeria and toxoplasmosis, and ask before taking medication. If you have bleeding, severe one-sided abdominal pain or dizziness, get in touch immediately.

## When to tell people

That’s up to you. Many wait until after week 12, because the risk of miscarriage falls then. You don’t have to tell anyone before you are ready.

Most complaints in pregnancy are harmless. But with the following signs you shouldn’t wait; contact your practice, the hospital or the emergency number 112 straight away.

## Act immediately if you have

- Vaginal bleeding
- Severe or persistent abdominal pain
- Leaking amniotic fluid (waters breaking) before week 37
- Regular contractions before week 37
- Noticeably fewer or no baby movements
- Severe headache, vision problems, flickering in front of the eyes
- Pain in the upper abdomen, especially on the right under the ribs
- Sudden swelling of the face and hands
- Fever above 38 °C
- Severe itching, especially on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet
- Severe, persistent vomiting, if you can’t keep anything down
- A burning feeling when passing urine with fever or pain in your side
- Pain, redness or swelling in one leg
- Shortness of breath or chest pain
- A fall, accident or blow to the belly, even if you feel fine

## In the first weeks

Severe, usually one-sided pain in the lower abdomen, shoulder pain, dizziness or fainting may indicate an ectopic pregnancy. This is an emergency: call 112 or have someone take you to a hospital immediately.

## Whom to call

- **Emergency number 112:** for heavy bleeding, shortness of breath, chest pain, unconsciousness, a seizure or after an accident.
- **Labour ward of your maternity hospital:** in the second half of pregnancy, for contractions, waters breaking, bleeding or fewer baby movements. It is staffed around the clock.
- **Gynaecologist’s practice:** during opening hours, for anything that shouldn’t wait until tomorrow.
- **Out-of-hours medical service 116 117:** at night and at weekends, if it isn’t an emergency but you need medical advice.

## What to say on the phone

Give your week of pregnancy, what has happened and since when. Have your maternity record ready. If you go to the hospital, take it with you and, if possible, don’t drive yourself.

## Better once too often

You are not bothering anyone. Labour wards take such calls seriously, and nobody expects you to judge for yourself whether something is dangerous. Under “Emergencies” in Babyliebe you’ll find all the important numbers, one tap away.

Most foods are allowed. Care is needed above all with raw animal products, because they can contain germs such as listeria, toxoplasma or salmonella.

## Better avoid

- Raw milk and cheese made from raw milk, except long-matured hard cheese such as Parmesan (remove the rind)
- Raw or undercooked meat, raw sausage such as salami or Mettwurst
- Raw fish (sushi), smoked or cured fish such as smoked salmon
- Raw eggs, for example in homemade mayonnaise or tiramisu
- Pre-cut, packaged salads and sprouts
- Alcohol – in any amount
- Liver in the first three months (very high in vitamin A)

## Allowed in moderation

- Coffee and black tea: up to 200 mg of caffeine a day, about two cups of coffee
- Tuna: rarely, because of possible mercury contamination
- Sweeteners: safe in usual amounts

## Simple rules

Cook meat, fish and eggs thoroughly. Wash fruit, vegetables and herbs thoroughly. Cool leftovers quickly and use them up soon. The food traffic light in Babyliebe helps you make a quick assessment.

## Toxoplasmosis

If you don’t know whether you are protected against toxoplasmosis, it’s especially important: no raw or undercooked meat, wear gloves for gardening and have someone else clean the cat litter tray every day. A test for it is optional and usually something you pay for yourself in Germany.

## Fish yes, but cooked

Sea fish once or twice a week is recommended, including oily fish such as salmon, mackerel or herring. It provides iodine and omega-3 fatty acids. What matters is that it is cooked thoroughly.

## Why it can be hard

Exhaustion makes you irritable. Almost all attention goes to the baby. Tasks are shared unequally; usually more work stays with the mother, even if both had planned it differently. Physical changes, hormones and worries add to this. Closeness and sexuality move into the background.

## What helps

- **Talk before things blow up:** talk briefly and honestly on a regular basis about how you are. A sentence like “I’m very tired right now and need a break” is better than accusations.
- **Share tasks:** agree who gets up when at night, who cooks, who shops. A plan prevents silence and resentment.
- **Small moments together:** ten minutes together on the sofa, a walk with the pram, a coffee, without phones.
- **Accept help:** grandparents, friends and neighbours, home help, family counselling. Health insurance also offers support if needed.
- **Tenderness:** closeness doesn’t have to mean sex. When you are ready again, take your time and talk about it.

## When one of you is under particular strain

Fathers and partners can also develop depressive symptoms after the birth. Signs are persistent low mood, irritability, withdrawal and exhaustion. It’s important to take this seriously and get help, for example from a GP, an advice centre or Telefonseelsorge (0800 111 0 111).

## Using counselling

Couples and family counselling is often free or inexpensive. In Germany, pregnancy advice centres provide support until the child’s third year of life. Getting support early is a sign of care.

## Free counselling

In Germany you are entitled to counselling from a pregnancy advice centre, even if you are not in a crisis situation. It is free, confidential and anonymous if you wish. The centres help with questions about money, housing, work and applications and support you in filling them out.

You can reach the “Schwangere in Not” helpline (pregnant women in need) around the clock on 0800 40 40 020, free and anonymous. If you experience violence at home, the “Gewalt gegen Frauen” helpline (violence against women) helps on 116 016. In acute danger, call the emergency number 112 or 110.

## Money in pregnancy and the postnatal period

- **Maternity protection and maternity pay:** if you are employed, the protection periods before and after the birth apply. Your health insurer pays maternity pay, and your employer usually pays a top-up. Ask your health insurer what applies to you.
- **Parental allowance:** under certain conditions, single parents can receive up to 14 months of basic parental allowance, because the partner months also stay with you. The parental allowance office of your federal state checks whether this applies to you.
- **Baby essentials:** if you receive citizen’s income (Bürgergeld), social assistance or have a low income, there are benefits for the initial equipment for pregnancy and birth, for example for clothing, a cot or a pram. They are applied for separately, ideally before you buy.
- **Federal foundation Mutter und Kind:** it supports pregnant women in financial hardship. You apply through a pregnancy advice centre.
- **Other benefits:** depending on your income, housing benefit, the child supplement or citizen’s income may be options. A counselling session shows you what suits you.

## Child maintenance and paternity

The other parent is obliged to pay maintenance for the child. If you are not married, the mother can also claim maintenance for a certain period around the birth and, if she looks after the child, beyond that. A counselling session clarifies how long and how much.

If the other parent doesn’t pay or pays too little, you can apply for maintenance advance (Unterhaltsvorschuss) at the youth welfare office. It applies to children up to their 12th birthday, for a maximum of 72 months in total, and is subject to further conditions.

The youth welfare office offers you free assistance (Beistandschaft). It helps with establishing paternity and enforcing maintenance. Paternity can already be acknowledged before the birth at the youth welfare office, registry office or a notary; this is also free.

## Custody

If the parents are not married, the mother initially has sole custody. Joint custody arises when both make a declaration of custody, which can be done free of charge at the youth welfare office. As long as there is no declaration of custody, you decide alone. Have the youth welfare office explain whether joint custody makes sense for you.

## Taxes

As a single parent you may be able to use tax class II and the relief allowance for single parents. Ask at the tax office or a wage tax assistance association.

## People who support you

- **Your midwife** cares for you during pregnancy and the postnatal period. Look for one early; in many regions they are booked up quickly.
- **Family midwives and Frühe Hilfen** support families in stressful situations. The offer is voluntary and usually free. The youth welfare office or the advice centre arranges it.
- **A network of friends and family:** say specifically what you need, for example meals in the postnatal period, someone to accompany you to the birth or someone to hold the baby while you shower.
- **Groups and meet-ups** for single parents exist in many places, for example through family centres.

## When everything gets too much

If you feel exhausted, lonely or overwhelmed, that is not a weakness. Talk to your midwife or your doctor. You can reach Telefonseelsorge around the clock on 0800 111 0 111 or 0800 111 0 222, free and anonymous.

A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy before week 24. It is more common than many think: about 10 to 20 in 100 known pregnancies end this way, most of them in the first twelve weeks.

## Why does it happen?

In most cases it is due to a chromosomal change in the embryo that prevents it from developing further. It is chance. Nothing you did or didn’t do caused it: not exercise, not a fright, not exertion, not sex.

## How do you recognise it?

Warning signs are bleeding, cramps in the lower abdomen or passing tissue. But light bleeding also occurs in healthy pregnancies. If you have bleeding with pain, heavier bleeding or fever, have yourself examined by a doctor promptly. If you have very heavy bleeding, dizziness or fainting, call 112.

## What happens physically?

If tissue remains, the body can expel it by itself, this can be supported with medication, or it can be removed in a short operation (curettage). You discuss which option suits you with your doctor. After a miscarriage you are entitled to midwife care. Your cycle usually returns within four to six weeks.

## Work and maternity protection

Since 1 June 2025, maternity protection also applies after a miscarriage: two weeks from week 13 of pregnancy, six weeks from week 17 and eight weeks from week 20. During this time you may not be employed unless you expressly state that you want to work. You can withdraw this at any time. Have your doctor certify the miscarriage and give the certificate to your employer. Before week 13, your doctor can sign you off sick if you need time.

## Grief is allowed

Some grieve deeply, others less. Both are fine. Even after very early miscarriages the loss can hurt, especially if you were already looking forward to your child. Rituals, talking with your partner, a midwife or a pastoral counsellor can help. Self-help groups and advice centres support you, such as the association “Verwaiste Eltern” (bereaved parents). Telefonseelsorge can be reached around the clock: 0800 111 0 111.

## A new pregnancy

A fixed waiting time is usually not medically necessary. What matters is that you are physically and emotionally ready. After a single miscarriage, the chance of a healthy pregnancy remains high. After repeated miscarriages (two or more), an assessment is worthwhile.

Pre-eclampsia is a condition that can occur after week 20 of pregnancy. It affects about 2 to 5 in 100 pregnant women. Typical signs are raised blood pressure and protein in the urine. It can endanger mother and child, but if recognised early it can be monitored and treated well.

## Why antenatal care is so important

At every antenatal appointment, blood pressure, urine and weight are checked. This allows many cases to be detected early, often before you notice anything yourself. That’s why you should definitely keep your appointments.

## Warning signs for which you should get medical help immediately

- severe or persistent headaches that don’t respond to painkillers
- vision problems such as flickering, flashes of light or blurred vision
- pain in the upper right abdomen or under the ribs
- sudden, severe swelling of the face and hands
- nausea or vomiting later in pregnancy
- sudden weight gain of more than one kilogram in a few days

If you have these signs, call your doctor, go to the hospital or call the out-of-hours medical service on 116 117. If you have seizures or severe symptoms, call 112.

## Who is particularly at risk?

Women who have had pre-eclampsia before have a higher risk, as do those with high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, multiple pregnancies, obesity or in a first pregnancy. If your risk is increased, your doctor may discuss preventive treatment with low-dose aspirin. Don’t take it without medical advice.

## Treatment

Treatment ranges from close monitoring and blood-pressure-lowering medication to delivery. The birth is the most effective treatment. The timing is carefully weighed up.

## HELLP syndrome

HELLP syndrome is a rare, serious form with changes in blood values and the liver. Severe upper abdominal pain is an alarm signal and must be checked immediately.

A twin pregnancy is something special – and is monitored a little more closely.

## Antenatal care

There are more ultrasound checks, especially if the twins share a placenta. Whether this is the case is best seen in the first trimester.

## Birth

On average, twins are born around weeks 36 to 37. Whether a vaginal birth is possible depends above all on the position of the first baby.

## Rights

After a multiple birth, maternity protection after the birth is extended to twelve weeks. Parental allowance includes a multiple-birth supplement of 300 euros for each additional child.

## Practical

Exchange experiences with other parents of multiples, plan for more support and get the baby essentials earlier.

## Know the warning signs

With twins, high blood pressure, gestational diabetes and premature contractions are more common. Get in touch immediately if you have bleeding, leaking amniotic fluid, regular contractions, severe headaches or if your bump gets noticeably bigger within a few days. In an emergency, call 112.

Some vaccinations protect not only you but, through your antibodies, also your newborn in the first months of life.

## Whooping cough (pertussis)

Recommended in every pregnancy, at the start of the third trimester; in the second trimester if there is an increased risk of premature birth. Whooping cough is dangerous for young babies.

## Flu (influenza)

Recommended from the second trimester, and from the first if you have a chronic condition – in each case during flu season.

## Not during pregnancy

Live vaccines such as measles-mumps-rubella or chickenpox are not given during pregnancy. Ideally, your immunity is checked before pregnancy.

It’s best to discuss which vaccinations make sense for you at your check-up. You’ll find current recommendations from the Robert Koch Institute.

## For the people around you

STIKO also recommends a whooping cough vaccination for your baby’s close contacts, such as partners, siblings and grandparents, if their last one was more than ten years ago. Ideally at least four weeks before the birth.

## For your baby after the birth

Against RSV, which can cause severe respiratory infections in babies, STIKO recommends an antibody for newborns in their first RSV season. Your paediatrician will discuss this with you, often already at the maternity hospital.

## Are vaccinations safe in pregnancy?

The recommended inactivated vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy. Mild reactions such as a sore arm are possible. Embryotox also provides independent information.

In Germany, parental allowance (Elterngeld) replaces part of your income while you look after your child after the birth. Parental leave is the release from work – the two are linked but applied for separately.

## Parental allowance

- Basic parental allowance: 65 to 67 percent of your net income before the birth, at least 300 and at most 1,800 euros a month.
- Both parents together have 14 months of basic parental allowance if both receive it. Receiving it at the same time is only possible for one month within the first twelve months of life.
- ElterngeldPlus: half as much, but for twice as long – ideal if you work part-time.
- Partnership bonus: extra months if both parents work 24 to 32 hours a week at the same time.

For births from April 2025, an income limit of 175,000 euros of taxable income per couple applies.

## Parental leave

Up to three years per child and parent. You must notify your employer in writing: no later than seven weeks before it begins.

## Application

Parental allowance is applied for after the birth at the parental allowance office – retrospectively for only three months. You’ll find the official calculator and the online application at familienportal.de.

## Maternity pay is offset

In the months after the birth in which you receive maternity pay, it is offset against your parental allowance. These months still count as your parental allowance months. Take this into account when dividing the months between you.

About one in 60 to 70 pregnancies in Germany is a twin pregnancy. It is something special and is monitored more closely than a pregnancy with one baby.

## Identical and non-identical

Non-identical twins develop from two fertilised eggs and are genetically like siblings. This is the case for about two thirds of twins. Identical twins develop when one fertilised egg divides early. They have the same genetic material.

## More important: placenta and amniotic sac

For care, what matters most is whether each baby has their own placenta (**dichorionic**) or both share one (**monochorionic**). This is best determined by ultrasound in the first trimester.

- **Dichorionic diamniotic:** two placentas, two amniotic sacs. All non-identical and some identical twins.
- **Monochorionic diamniotic:** one placenta, two amniotic sacs. They are checked about every two weeks.
- **Monochorionic monoamniotic:** one placenta, one amniotic sac. Rare, and monitored especially closely.

## What’s different in the care

There are more ultrasound scans and checks. Antenatal care is often provided by a practice or centre with experience of multiples. The birth is best in a hospital that can care for twins and premature babies.

## Important to know

Most twin pregnancies go well. Take your appointments seriously, mention any uncertainty early and get help. With warning signs such as bleeding, leaking amniotic fluid, regular contractions, severe headaches or a rapidly increasing bump, call your practice or hospital immediately, in an emergency 112.

About one in ten pregnant women develops gestational diabetes. It usually causes no symptoms but can affect the baby’s growth. That’s why a test is offered between weeks 24 and 28.

## How the test works

- Screening test: you drink a sugar solution with 50 g of glucose, and blood is taken after one hour. You don’t need to fast for this.
- If the value is abnormal, a diagnostic test with 75 g of glucose follows, this time fasting, with three blood samples.

## If you are diagnosed

Usually an adjusted diet and more exercise are enough. You then measure your own blood sugar. Only some women need insulin. After the birth the values almost always return to normal – a follow-up test a few weeks later is still important.

## For your baby

When well controlled, a pregnancy with gestational diabetes usually goes without problems. After the birth, your baby’s blood sugar is checked a few times because it can be too low in the first hours. Early and frequent breastfeeding helps with this.

## For you later on

Women who had gestational diabetes have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes later in life. So have a glucose test after the birth and your blood sugar checked regularly afterwards. Exercise and breastfeeding lower the risk.

You record your values in a diary, which the diabetes team discusses with you regularly. Babyliebe has a blood sugar diary for this that you can take to your appointments.

About one in three babies in Germany is born by caesarean section. Sometimes it is planned, for example if the baby is lying sideways; sometimes it becomes necessary during labour.

## Procedure

Usually a spinal or epidural anaesthetic is given, so you are awake and can see your baby straight away. The operation takes about 30 to 45 minutes, and the baby is often born within a few minutes. A birth partner is usually allowed to be present.

## Wishes

Ask whether bonding in theatre is possible, whether the screen can be lowered for the birth and whether your baby can stay with your birth partner while you are being cared for.

## Recovery

You can usually get up on the same day. Taking it easy is important: no heavy lifting for six to eight weeks. Postnatal care from your midwife applies just as it does after a vaginal birth.

## Everyday life afterwards

The scar usually heals well. Keep it clean and dry and have your midwife look at it. Breastfeeding works just as well after a caesarean; lying on your side or the rugby-ball hold protect your belly. Discuss with your doctor when you can drive again.

Fever is the body’s defence reaction to an infection. It worries you, but it is usually a sign that the immune system is working. More important than how high it is, is how your baby is doing overall.

## Measuring fever

The most reliable method is measuring in the bottom (rectally) with a digital thermometer. Ear and forehead thermometers are less accurate in young babies. A temperature from 38.0 degrees rectally counts as fever; between 37.5 and 37.9 degrees counts as a raised temperature.

## When to see a doctor immediately?

- for babies **under three months**, with any temperature from 38.0 degrees, on the same day
- for all babies and children, with a fever above 39 degrees that doesn’t come down, or a fever that lasts longer than three days
- with difficulty breathing, very fast breathing, the skin pulling in between the ribs
- if your baby is feeding poorly, has hardly any wet nappies, dry lips or signs of dehydration
- with listlessness, unusual drowsiness, high-pitched crying or sensitivity to touch
- with a seizure
- with a rash that doesn’t fade when pressed (glass test) and your baby seems very unwell

In these cases, contact the practice, call the out-of-hours medical service on 116 117 or, if life is in danger, 112.

## What helps?

Offer plenty to drink, breast milk or the bottle on demand, light clothing, a pleasant room temperature of around 18 to 20 degrees, rest and closeness. Wrapping your baby up warmly doesn’t make sense.

## Fever-reducing medication

It is usually only needed if your baby feels very unwell. Paracetamol or ibuprofen as suppositories or syrup are dosed by body weight and only given after consulting your paediatrician; for babies under three months only on a doctor’s advice. Cold calf wraps are no longer recommended for babies.

A mild fever can occur after vaccinations. It subsides after one to two days. If the fever is high or things get worse, call the practice.

## During pregnancy

- Explain what’s happening in an age-appropriate way: a baby is growing in the belly and will arrive in a few months. Young children don’t yet understand periods of time, so link it to events such as “when winter comes”.
- Let your child stroke the bump, look at ultrasound pictures and look at picture books about siblings.
- Involve them in the preparations: they can choose clothes or a present for the baby.
- Take them along to an antenatal appointment or the midwife’s visit.
- Discuss who will look after them when labour starts.

## Changes before, not after

If your child is to move out of the parents’ bed, give up the pram or start nursery, do it in good time before the birth. That way they don’t associate the change with the baby.

## In the hospital and afterwards

A visit to the hospital is often lovely. A present “from the baby” helps at the first meeting. At home, plan time just with the older child, even if it is short. Involve them in changing or dressing the baby without pressuring them.

## Jealousy

Setbacks such as wetting, baby talk or defiance are normal. Your child is showing that they need closeness. Take feelings seriously (“You’re angry because I’m so busy with the baby”), set clear limits (don’t hurt the baby) and give lots of attention. Never leave children alone with a baby unsupervised.

## The partner

A second parent who spends time with the older child is especially valuable in the early days. It creates stability and takes the pressure off.

Being carried corresponds to what newborns need: closeness, warmth, heartbeat and movement. Carrying calms many babies and makes everyday life easier for you, because your hands are free.

## The right position

The **M position** (spread-squat position) is important: the legs are bent and slightly spread, the knees are higher than the bottom, and the fabric reaches from the back of one knee to the other. The back is rounded and the head is close enough to kiss, so you can give your baby a kiss on the forehead. This position is good for the hips.

## Sling or carrier?

- **Sling:** adjustable to any size, gives a lot of support, but tying it takes practice. Especially suitable for newborns.
- **Carrier with a panel (soft structured carrier):** quick to put on, suitable for newborns with an insert or newborn mode, and comfortable for longer carrying later.

It’s best to get instructions from a babywearing consultant or your midwife. Many offer classes.

## Safety rules for babywearing

- **Tight enough:** your baby is held firmly and doesn’t slump down.
- **Always in view:** the face stays uncovered and isn’t covered by fabric or your body.
- **Close enough to kiss:** the head is high enough for you to kiss.
- **Chin free:** the chin doesn’t rest on the chest, so the airways stay open.
- **Back supported:** the back is rounded and well held.

## What else to look out for

Don’t carry your baby while cooking at the stove, with hot drinks or while cycling. Don’t dress your baby too warmly, because you keep each other warm. If there is pain or discomfort, change the position.

Make sure the weight is carried close to your body and well distributed. After a caesarean or if you have pelvic floor problems, discuss carrying with your midwife.

Midwives support you during pregnancy, at the birth and until the end of breastfeeding. In Germany, statutory and usually also private health insurance covers the costs.

## What midwives do

- Antenatal check-ups, also alternating with the doctor’s practice
- Help with complaints such as nausea or back pain
- Antenatal classes
- Support during the birth
- Postnatal care at home: daily in the first ten days, then as needed
- Breastfeeding advice and postnatal recovery classes

## How to find one

Ask early, ideally in the first trimester. Helpful sources are your regional midwives’ association search, recommendations from people around you and the maternity hospitals near you. Save your midwife’s number in Babyliebe under “Important contacts”.

## What health insurance pays for

- Check-ups and help with complaints during pregnancy
- An antenatal class of up to 14 hours
- Home visits in the postnatal period up to twelve weeks after the birth
- After that, help with breastfeeding problems and feeding questions for as long as you breastfeed
- A postnatal recovery class

## Can’t find a midwife?

Ask your health insurer, your maternity hospital and midwife coordination centres in your region. Some hospitals offer a midwife consultation or a postnatal outpatient clinic. You’ll find the midwife list of the GKV-Spitzenverband under “Find help”.

Even if you can’t find a midwife for the pregnancy, it’s worth searching for the postnatal period. Many still take on women at short notice for this.

## The right position

From the third trimester, lying on your side is the most comfortable and best for blood flow. Left or right – both are fine. If you wake up on your back, simply turn onto your side again.

## Aids

- A pillow between your knees relieves your hips and back
- A nursing pillow supports your bump and back at the same time
- A slightly raised head end helps with heartburn

## Evening routine

Avoid large meals and drinking a lot shortly before bed, put your phone away earlier and try relaxation or breathing exercises. A short nap during the day helps make up for bad nights.

## Restless legs

Tingling and restlessness in the legs in the evening are common in the last trimester. Exercise, stretching and warmth help. Sometimes iron deficiency is behind it – mention it at your check-up.

## When worries keep you awake

Write down what’s on your mind and take it to your next appointment. Breathing exercises and the meditations in Babyliebe can help you fall asleep. If worries and sleeplessness go on for weeks, talk to your midwife or doctor.

Many pregnant women dream more intensely than usual. This is normal and is related to hormones and waking up more often.

In an antenatal class you learn what happens during the birth and how you can prepare for it. The classes are usually run by midwives.

## Content

- The course of labour and its stages
- Breathing and relaxation techniques, positions during labour
- Options for pain relief
- The first days with your baby, breastfeeding and the postnatal period
- Exchange with other pregnant women

## When and how

Classes usually start between weeks 25 and 30 – you should book earlier. There are weekly courses, weekend courses and online options.

## Costs

In Germany, health insurance covers the cost of up to 14 hours for you. Some insurers voluntarily pay for partners – ask.

## For partners

Many classes have separate sessions for birth partners or are designed entirely as couples’ classes. There you learn how you can give concrete support during the birth, for example with massage, positions and breathing.

## Other formats

There are classes for women who already have a child, classes focusing on caesarean birth or relaxation, and one-to-one sessions with your midwife. Ask what is on offer near you and what health insurance pays for.

It’s best to sign up in the second trimester; especially in cities, classes are booked up early.

In Germany you can choose where your child is born. There is no “right” or “wrong”, but the decision depends on your pregnancy, your wishes and what is available locally.

## Hospital

Most children are born in hospitals. Advantages are round-the-clock medical care, paediatricians and anaesthetists on site and all options for pain relief. For high-risk pregnancies or premature births, the hospital is the right choice. Hospitals differ greatly in atmosphere, caesarean rate, staffing ratio and what they offer.

## Birth centre

Birth centres are run by midwives. The atmosphere is more homely, and you are usually cared for by the same midwife. They are an option for healthy women with an uncomplicated pregnancy. If complications arise, you are transferred to a hospital. That’s why the hospital should be within easy reach.

## Home birth

At a home birth, the midwife comes to you. This too is suitable for healthy pregnant women with an uneventful pregnancy. You stay in familiar surroundings, but you need to know that a transfer to hospital will be necessary if complications arise. A plan for this case is part of it.

## Questions for your visit

- How many births are there per year, and what is the caesarean rate?
- Can I register in advance and see the labour ward?
- Which pain relief options and birth positions are possible?
- Can my birth partner be there the whole time?
- How does postnatal care work, are there family rooms and rooming-in?
- What happens in an emergency or a transfer?

## What to keep in mind

Choose the place where you feel safe, and stay flexible. If something changes along the way, switching is not a failure. Early contact with a midwife and registering in good time help.

During pregnancy your body produces significantly more blood to supply you and your baby. For this it needs more iron. In the second and third trimester, the requirement is roughly twice as high as usual.

## How do you recognise a deficiency?

Typical signs are unusual tiredness, paleness, shortness of breath, dizziness, headaches, palpitations or brittle nails. Since many of these complaints also occur in a normal pregnancy, the haemoglobin level (Hb) in the blood is checked regularly at antenatal appointments. If it shows a deficiency, the ferritin level, which describes the iron stores, is usually measured.

## Diet

Good sources of iron are meat (especially red meat), pulses, wholegrain products, oats, millet, pumpkin seeds and green vegetables. Iron from plant sources is absorbed better if you eat vitamin C at the same time, for example peppers, orange juice or berries. Coffee, black tea, dairy products and calcium supplements inhibit absorption and shouldn’t be drunk right with an iron-rich meal.

## Iron supplements

Whether you need a supplement is decided by your doctor based on your blood values. Don’t take iron on suspicion or in high doses without consulting your doctor. Possible side effects are nausea, constipation and dark stools. If you don’t tolerate them well, there are other preparations and times to take them. If the deficiency is severe, iron by infusion is also an option.

## Why is it important?

Severe anaemia can wear you down and lead to a higher risk if you lose blood during the birth. Well-filled iron stores also make the time after the birth easier.

## Important

Not all tiredness is iron deficiency. Have your blood values checked instead of treating yourself.

In a healthy pregnancy, sex is allowed until the birth. Your baby is well protected by the amniotic sac, the amniotic fluid and the closed cervix.

## What changes

Desire can fluctuate – sometimes more, sometimes less. That’s normal. As your bump grows, other positions become more comfortable, such as lying on your side.

## When you should take a break

- If there is bleeding
- With premature contractions or a shortened cervix
- If the placenta is lying in front of the cervix
- After your waters have broken

If your doctor recommends a break, ask what exactly is meant. Closeness and tenderness are possible without sex too.

## After the birth

You decide when you have sex again. Many women wait until the lochia has eased and injuries have healed. Due to hormonal changes, especially when breastfeeding, the vagina can be drier. Lubricant helps.

## Contraception

You can become pregnant again even before your first period after the birth. Breastfeeding alone isn’t reliable protection. At your postnatal check, talk to your doctor about which contraception suits you.

Light bleeding after sex can happen because the cervix has a greater blood supply. It is usually harmless. Still, contact your practice if the bleeding is heavier or you have pain as well.

Talk openly about what feels good for both of you. Changes in desire are not a sign of problems in your relationship.

Every birth is different. Still, it follows typical stages. Knowing what’s coming can take away some of the fear.

## First stage (opening)

The contractions open the cervix to about ten centimetres. This is the longest stage – often many hours for a first birth. Movement, warmth, breathing and changing position help.

## Transition

The contractions are now very intense, and many women feel exhausted or overwhelmed. This is normal and a sign that things will soon move on.

## Second stage (pushing)

The baby’s head moves lower and you feel a strong urge to push. With the pushing contractions your baby is born. This stage usually lasts between a few minutes and two hours.

## Third stage (placenta)

The placenta is delivered within about 30 minutes. Ideally your baby is already lying on your chest by then. Afterwards, checks are made to see whether any injuries need treating.

## When to set off

When it’s time to go to the hospital is described in the guide “Is it starting? The signs of labour”. If in doubt, always call ahead.

## After the birth

You usually stay in the labour ward for the first two hours. Your baby lies on your chest, is examined for the first time (U1) and can feed for the first time if they want to. Bleeding and circulation are closely monitored during this time.

Mit der Beikost beginnt für dein Baby ei:
Starting solids begins a new phase for your baby: they learn that there are many other tastes besides milk. It’s not only about getting full, but also about discovering.

## When is it time?

According to the recommendations of the German network Gesund ins Leben, solids should start at the earliest at the beginning of the 5th month and at the latest at the beginning of the 7th month. The 2026 German breastfeeding guideline recommends exclusive or predominant breastfeeding for about six months. The German professional association of paediatricians and the guideline on allergy prevention still consider starting from the fifth month to be right. Talk to your paediatrician or midwife about what suits you.

More important than the exact age are signs of readiness: your baby can sit upright with support, holds their head steady, shows interest in food, and the tongue-thrust reflex, which pushes food back out, has disappeared.

## The classic way: purées

1. **Vegetable, potato and meat purée** (from about month 5 to 7): with carrot, pumpkin, parsnip or broccoli, plus cooked meat and a spoonful of oil (for example rapeseed oil). Meat provides iron and zinc.
2. **Milk and cereal purée** (about a month later): wholegrain cereal flakes with milk (small amounts) or breast milk, with fruit.
3. **Cereal and fruit purée** (another month later): without milk, with fruit purée.

This is how you gradually replace milk feeds. Breastfeeding or the bottle remains important alongside.

## Baby-led weaning

With “baby-led weaning”, your baby feeds themselves soft pieces they can grasp right from the start. What matters is an upright position, constant supervision and suitable foods: cooked vegetable sticks, soft pieces of fruit, bread crust. Make sure to include sources of iron such as meat, lentils or wholegrains.

## What’s not allowed?

- Honey (infant botulism) in the first year
- Whole nuts, grapes, raw carrots, popcorn: risk of choking
- As little salt and sugar as possible
- Raw milk, raw meat and raw eggs
- Cow’s milk as the main drink before the first birthday

## Allergens

According to the current guideline, you don’t need to avoid potential allergens such as egg, peanut (as a smooth paste), fish and wheat. Introduce them in small amounts in the first year with solids. If your baby has eczema or there are allergies in the family, talk to your paediatrician.

## Patience

New tastes often need ten to fifteen attempts. Your child decides how much they eat. Pressure and distraction don’t help.

Mit einer abwechslungsreichen Ernährung:
A varied diet gives you almost everything you and your baby need. But two nutrients should be taken in addition.

## Folic acid

Folic acid reduces the risk of malformations of the neural tube, from which the brain and spinal cord develop. 400 µg daily as a tablet is recommended – ideally from four weeks before conception and at least until the end of the first trimester.

## Iodine

Your baby needs iodine for the development of the thyroid gland and brain. 100 to 150 µg daily as a tablet is recommended, in addition to iodised table salt. If you have a thyroid condition, check with your doctor first.

## Only if needed

- Iron: only if a deficiency has been found in your blood.
- Vitamin D: often useful in winter; talk to your doctor.
- Omega-3 fatty acids (DHA): oily sea fish once or twice a week, or a supplement with at least 200 mg of DHA.
- Vegan diet: be sure to supplement vitamin B12 and have it monitored by a doctor.

High-dose combination products “for pregnant women” are usually not necessary. It’s best to take supplements after talking to your doctor.

## If you are already pregnant

If you didn’t take folic acid before the pregnancy, simply start now. The greatest benefit is in the first weeks, but starting later still makes sense.

## While breastfeeding

Iodine remains important while breastfeeding because it reaches your baby through your milk. The recommendation for a tablet therefore continues for as long as you breastfeed. If you have a thyroid condition, discuss the dose with your doctor.

Talk to your child a lot, name things, read aloud and sing. At two years, about 50 words and first two-word sentences are typical.
