Mit wenigen Regeln senkst du das Risiko:
With a few rules you can significantly lower the risk of sudden infant death. They apply throughout the first year of life, especially in the first six months.

## The most important rules

- Always put your baby to sleep on their back, including for naps
- In their own cot or a bedside cot in the parents’ bedroom, during the first year of life
- A firm, flat mattress; no pillows, cot bumpers, blankets, sheepskins or soft toys in the cot
- A baby sleeping bag in the right size instead of a blanket; the head stays uncovered
- Room temperature of about 16 to 18 degrees; don’t dress your baby too warmly, no hat in the cot
- A smoke-free environment, during pregnancy and afterwards, including at home and in the car

## Not too warm

Whether your baby is sweating or cold is best felt on the back of the neck, not on the hands or feet. If the neck is damp and warm, take off a layer.

## On their back, even when they roll

Lying on the side is not safe, because babies roll onto their tummy from it. If your baby later rolls from back to tummy and back again by themselves, you may leave them like that. But always put them down on their back. Playing on their tummy is good for development, but only when your baby is awake and you are there.

## Breastfeeding and dummies

Breastfeeding protects. A dummy when falling asleep can also protect; if you are breastfeeding, ideally only once breastfeeding is going well. If it falls out during sleep, you don’t need to put it back in.

## In the parents’ bed

If you sleep together in one bed, it is especially important: no smoking, no alcohol and no medication or drugs that make you drowsy. The baby lies on their back, without the adults’ pillows and duvet.

## Never on a sofa or armchair

Falling asleep together on a sofa or in an armchair is especially dangerous. If you notice you are getting tired, put your baby in their cot.

## When out and about

Infant carriers and car seats are designed for travelling, not as a bed. In a sling or carrier, the face stays uncovered and the chin doesn’t rest on the chest.

## Emergency

If your baby isn’t breathing, is floppy or turning blue, call 112 immediately. The control centre will explain on the phone what you can do.
Mit zwei Babys ist vieles doppelt: Winde:
With two babies, a lot is doubled: nappies, feeds, sleep. With some planning and support, everyday life becomes manageable.

## Breastfeeding

Many mothers breastfeed both babies. It can be done at the same time, for example in the double cradle hold or the rugby-ball hold with pillows, or one after the other. Ask your midwife or a lactation consultant about positions. A combination of breastfeeding and the bottle is also fine. What matters is that you stay fed and rested.

## One rhythm for both

When one baby wakes up, wake the other for a feed too. Then both are on the same schedule and you get longer breaks. Keep a record, for example in the app, of who fed when.

## Safe sleep

The rules apply to each baby: on their back, a firm mattress, no pillow, no blanket and no cot bumper, a room temperature of 16 to 18 degrees. Each baby should lie in their own cot. If you have questions about co-sleeping, talk to your paediatrician or midwife.

## Baby essentials

You need many things twice, but not everything. For prams, car seats and cots, it’s worth checking second-hand or borrowed options. Several items of clothing in the same size save time.

## Help and money

- After the birth, your midwife looks after you.
- If no one can run the household, health insurance can pay for home help. This requires a doctor’s prescription.
- Parental allowance: for twins there is a multiple-birth supplement of 300 euros a month.
- Exchanging experiences with other parents of multiples helps and takes the pressure off.

Exhaustion is common with twins. If you feel low or overwhelmed for a long time, talk to your midwife or doctor. You can reach Telefonseelsorge free of charge on 0800 111 0 111.
Mit zwei Kindern steigt dein Bedarf an E:
With two babies, your need for energy, protein, iron, folic acid and calcium rises more than with one. At the same time, nausea or little room in your belly can make eating harder.

## Guide values for weight gain

For twins, the US Institute of Medicine (IOM) gives the following as a guide:

- women of normal weight: about 17 to 25 kilograms
- overweight women: about 14 to 23 kilograms
- women with obesity: about 11 to 19 kilograms

These are guide values from studies. How much is right for you is something you clarify with your doctor or midwife. Too little weight gain in the first half may be linked to a lower birth weight of the babies.

## What can help you with eating

- Eat five to six smaller meals instead of a few large ones.
- Focus on protein-rich and nutrient-rich foods such as dairy products, pulses, wholegrains, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts.
- Drink enough water and unsweetened teas.
- For heartburn, small portions and sitting upright after eating help.

## Nutrients

Discuss folic acid, iodine and, if needed, iron, vitamin D and omega-3 with your doctor. Don’t take high-dose supplements on your own initiative. Iron levels are often checked more frequently with twins.

## Keeping an eye on your weight

Use the weight diary and discuss the curve with your care team. It can help you see whether you are gaining enough.

Muttermilch ist die natürliche Ernährung:
Breast milk is the natural food for your baby. But breastfeeding has to be learned – by both of you. Support is normal and important.

## The first hour

If possible, place your baby skin to skin on your chest straight after the birth. Most babies then search for the breast by themselves and feed for the first time.

## The first days

- In the first days, the first milk (colostrum) is produced – a small amount, but very nourishing.
- Around the third day the milk comes in, and the breasts become firm and warm.
- Feed your baby on demand, usually eight to twelve times in 24 hours.

## Latching on properly

Your baby lies tummy to tummy with you and takes a large part of the areola into their mouth. Pain while breastfeeding is a sign that the position isn’t quite right yet – ask your midwife or a lactation consultant.

## If breastfeeding doesn’t work

You can be close to your baby with a bottle too. You decide what’s right for you.

## Is my baby getting enough?

This is shown by wet nappies – from about day five usually five to six a day – regular stools and weight. Babies lose a little weight in the first days and usually regain their birth weight after 10 to 14 days.

## Getting help

Your midwife helps you with all breastfeeding questions in the postnatal period. There are also lactation consultants and breastfeeding groups. You’ll find places to turn to under “Find help”.

A lot changes after the birth: hormones, sleep, responsibility. Besides the baby blues and depression, there are conditions that are talked about less often. Knowing about them helps you get help earlier, and all of them are very treatable.

## Anxiety and worries that won’t go away

Worrying about your baby is normal. But if anxiety dominates the whole day, you can hardly relax, you have a racing heart or panic, or you constantly have to check whether your baby is breathing, an anxiety disorder may be behind it. Talk to your midwife or doctor about it.

## Distressing thoughts you don’t want

Many mothers experience sudden thoughts or images that something could happen to the baby or that they themselves could harm it, for example by dropping it. These thoughts are so frightening precisely because you don’t want them and want to protect your baby. Intrusive thoughts like these are common and don’t mean you will act on them.

If the thoughts weigh on you heavily, you avoid things because of them, such as bathing your baby, or you hardly dare to be alone with your baby any more, get support. This is very treatable, and you don’t need to feel ashamed.

## Postpartum psychosis: an emergency

Rarely, in about one or two in a thousand births, a psychosis develops, usually in the first days or weeks after the birth. Signs include:

- Confusion, great restlessness, hardly any sleep without feeling tired
- Hearing voices or seeing things that others don’t perceive
- Firm beliefs that others can’t follow
- Strongly changing moods, unusual behaviour

Often partners or family notice it first. Then don’t wait: call emergency number 112 straight away or go to the nearest psychiatric emergency department. With treatment, most women make a full recovery. If you have had a psychosis or bipolar disorder before, talk to your doctor about it already during pregnancy.

## When you need help immediately

If you feel the urge to harm yourself or your baby, or can no longer tell whether thoughts are just thoughts: call 112. In an emotional crisis you can reach Telefonseelsorge around the clock on 0800 111 0 111.

Your midwife, your gynaecologist or GP, the association Schatten & Licht with a list of specialists and self-help groups, and the Frühe Hilfen (early support services) in your town. Partners can also become ill after the birth and are allowed to seek help too.

Not every couple gets pregnant straight away. About 80 to 85 in 100 couples succeed within a year with regular sex in the fertile window. If it doesn’t work, it is often just a question of time; sometimes there is a treatable cause behind it.

## When to get checked?

After twelve months without a pregnancy, professional societies recommend an assessment. From age 35, already after six months. Earlier if you already know about possible causes, for example very irregular cycles, endometriosis, abdominal surgery or, in men, testicular conditions.

## What is examined?

For the **woman**, the focus is on cycle history, hormone levels, ultrasound and, if needed, checking the fallopian tubes. For the **man**, a semen analysis is carried out: the number, motility and shape of the sperm. In about a third of cases the cause lies with the woman, in a third with the man, and in the rest with both or remains unexplained.

## Possible treatments

Depending on the cause, options include cycle-regulating treatment, triggering ovulation, insemination (sperm is placed in the womb), in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). They are offered at fertility centres, which also support you with counselling.

## Costs

Under certain conditions, statutory health insurers in Germany cover part of the costs, for example for married couples, within certain age limits and with a treatment plan. The federal government and some states offer additional grants. Ask your insurer about the current conditions before starting treatment.

## For your mental health

Involuntary childlessness is a great burden. Talk about your feelings, give yourself breaks and seek psychosocial counselling if needed. Many fertility centres and advice centres offer it. You are not alone.

Emergencies with babies are rare, but hardly anything is as frightening. A paediatric first aid course gives you confidence. Many midwives, hospitals and aid organisations offer them for expectant parents. This text doesn’t replace a course.

## Emergency number 112

Call **112** immediately if your baby isn’t breathing, turns blue, doesn’t respond, has a seizure that doesn’t stop, is unconscious after a fall, or in the case of burns, poisoning or heavy bleeding. Say: **where** the emergency is, **what** has happened, **how many** people are affected, **which** injuries there are, and **wait** for questions.

## Choking

If your baby can no longer breathe, cough or cry:

1. Lay them face down along your forearm with the head lower, holding the head securely.
2. Give **five firm blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
3. Turn them over and press **five times with two fingers** in the middle of the chest.
4. Repeat until the object comes out or your baby breathes again. Ask someone to call 112.

## Resuscitation

If your baby doesn’t respond and isn’t breathing normally: call 112, give five rescue breaths (your mouth over their mouth and nose), then 30 chest compressions with two fingers in the middle of the chest, about a third of its depth, alternating with two rescue breaths. Don’t give up until help arrives. This is best learned in a course.

## Febrile seizure

A seizure can occur with fever. Stay calm, lay your baby on the floor or in a safe position, protect them from injury, and don’t put anything in their mouth. If it lasts longer than five minutes or it is the first seizure, call 112.

## Scalds and burns

Cool the affected areas immediately with running lukewarm water for about ten minutes. Only remove clothing if it isn’t stuck. No ointments, no ice. For an area larger than the palm of a hand, or on the face: 112.

## Poisoning

If you suspect poisoning (medication, cleaning products, plants): don’t make your baby vomit, don’t give anything to drink, keep the packaging ready and call the poison control centre or 112.

## Prevention

Keep small parts, medication and cleaning products out of reach, never leave your baby alone on the changing table or in the bath, and secure water and hobs.

Whether you bottle-feed in addition to breastfeeding or exclusively: you can experience loving feeding this way too. There are many reasons for the bottle, and none of them needs an explanation.

## Which formula?

For babies without particular needs, **first infant formula** (in Germany “Pre” or stage 1) is enough for the whole first year. It is the most similar to breast milk and can be given on demand. Follow-on milk is not necessary. Formulas for babies at risk of allergy (hypoallergenic, HA) only make sense for a medical reason. Follow the instructions on the packet exactly and don’t change anything by feel.

## Hygiene and preparation

- Wash your hands thoroughly, clean bottles and teats after every use with hot water and washing-up liquid, and let them dry well. In the first months, boiling or steam sterilising can also be useful.
- Let freshly boiled water cool to at least 70 degrees, not below, so that germs in the powder are killed.
- First pour in the water, then add the powder according to the instructions, without heaping the scoop. Shake until everything has dissolved.
- Before feeding, check the temperature on your wrist; it should be about body temperature.
- Throw away leftovers after one hour at most and don’t reheat them.

## How much?

In the first weeks, babies drink about 60 to 90 millilitres per feed and gradually increase the amount. Guide values are helpful, but your baby knows when they are full. Watch for signs: turning their head away, letting go of the teat, becoming calm.

## Closeness while feeding

Hold your baby in your arms, with eye contact, skin to skin if you like. Switch sides as you would when breastfeeding. Don’t leave your baby alone in bed with a bottle, otherwise there is a risk of choking and tooth decay. Partners can also feed and experience a special closeness this way.

## Teats and bottles

Choose a teat with the right hole size for your baby’s age. A teat that flows too fast leads to choking. Replace teats and bottles if they are cracked or discoloured.

Prenatal diagnostic tests are optional. They can give indications of certain conditions – but no guarantee of a healthy child. You have a right not to know.

## Non-invasive methods

- First-trimester screening (11+0 to 13+6): ultrasound of the nuchal translucency plus blood values, giving a probability. Usually self-pay.
- NIPT (blood test): examines fragments of the baby’s DNA in the mother’s blood for trisomy 13, 18 and 21. Health insurance pays for it if you and your doctor together conclude that the test makes sense in your situation.
- Detailed ultrasound (anomaly scan): a targeted examination of the organs, usually around week 20.

## Invasive methods

Amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling provide reliable diagnoses but carry a small risk of miscarriage. They are usually only considered after abnormal findings.

## Counselling

You are entitled to free, independent psychosocial counselling – before, during and after the tests, for example at pregnancy counselling centres.

## Before you decide

Think beforehand about what you would do with a result and whether you want to know at all. A normal result doesn’t rule out every condition. An abnormal result is usually not yet a diagnosis and needs further investigation.

You can decline any of these tests, even if they are offered to you. This has no effect on the rest of your antenatal care.

Regular exercise is good for you and your baby. It can ease back pain, lower the risk of gestational diabetes and build stamina for the birth.

## How much

At least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week is recommended, spread over several days. Moderate means you start to sweat but can still hold a conversation.

## Well suited

- Brisk walking, walking, cycling on safe routes
- Swimming and aqua fitness
- Pregnancy yoga and Pilates
- Light strength training

## Better avoid

- Sports with a risk of falls or impact, for example martial arts, horse riding, skiing
- Diving
- From the second trimester, long exercises lying on your back

## Stop immediately if you have

Bleeding, abdominal pain, leaking amniotic fluid, dizziness, shortness of breath before exertion or regular contractions. If you have a pre-existing condition or risks, talk to your doctor beforehand.

## If you haven’t done much exercise so far

Start slowly, for example with ten minutes of brisk walking a day, and build up. Taking the stairs instead of the lift and short journeys on foot also count.

## When you should ask first

Even the drive home from the hospital is a first car journey. A suitable, correctly installed seat is therefore one of the most important purchases.

## Car seat

Child seats in Europe must be approved according to the **UN R129 (i-Size)** standard or the older **ECE R44**. Keep in mind:

- **Rear-facing:** children should travel rear-facing for as long as possible, at least until 15 months. Head and neck are then better protected in an impact.
- **Fit:** the seat must fit your car and be properly secured. Try it in your car at a specialist shop and have them show you how to install it.
- **Harness:** the straps sit snugly, without thick clothing underneath (put thick jackets over the top).
- **Don’t buy second-hand** if you don’t know the seat’s history, because accident damage isn’t visible.
- If the passenger airbag is active, a rear-facing seat must not be placed there.

## Never alone in the car

Never leave your baby in the car, not even for a short time. In summer, a car heats up dangerously within minutes. Break up long journeys in the infant carrier with breaks, at least every one to two hours, so your baby can lie flat.

## Pram

Choose a pram with a **flat lying surface** for the first months, because newborns should lie flat. Look for good suspension, safety straps, a lockable brake and a height that suits your back. Try it with a full bag and folded in your car boot. Don’t hang heavy bags on the handle.

## Carrying or pushing?

The two complement each other. In the first weeks, a baby often sleeps well in the pram, while some babies calm down better in a sling. An infant carrier is not a substitute for a bed and isn’t meant for sleeping outside the car.

## Bicycle

You don’t cycle with a baby. Bike seats are only suitable from about nine to twelve months, when your child can sit securely and a helmet fits. Trailers with an infant carrier insert may be possible earlier; check the manufacturer’s information.

## In everyday life

- Take over tasks: shopping, carrying, cleaning with cleaning products, the cat’s litter tray
- Come along to antenatal appointments and scans
- Listen – share worries and joy

## Planning together

Find out about parental allowance and parental leave together, choose a midwife and hospital, and write the birth plan together. Think early about how you want to share tasks after the birth.

## At the birth

You are support, advocate and a calming presence. Know the birth plan, keep an eye on breaks, drinks and food – for yourself too.

## And you?

Partners can also have fears or go through a crisis after the birth. Talk about it and get support.

## After the birth

Skin-to-skin contact is good for you and your baby too. Take over changing, bathing and carrying from the start; this is how your bond grows. Partner months in the parental allowance make time together easier.

Look after yourself too: lack of sleep, worries about money or your job and a changed relationship are normal. You can find help, for example, from the parents’ helpline (Elterntelefon) and at advice centres.

Save the numbers of the hospital, the midwife and the emergency services on your phone too, and know the way to the hospital.

Feel free to ask if you don’t understand something at appointments.

Stillen ist natürlich, aber nicht immer:
Breastfeeding is natural, but not always easy. Almost all women face challenges in the first weeks. Most can be solved with good support.

## Sore nipples

The most common cause is a latching technique that isn’t quite right: the baby only takes the nipple instead of a large part of the areola. A wide-open mouth, a chin close to the breast and lips turned outwards are good signs. Have your midwife or lactation consultant show you. Between feeds it helps to let a little breast milk dry on the nipple or to use lanolin. Severe pain, cracks or bleeding are not a reason to grit your teeth, but a reason to get help.

## Blocked ducts

A blocked duct shows up as a hard, red, painful spot in the breast, sometimes with a slight fever. Feeding often, with your baby’s chin pointing towards the affected area, warmth before feeding and cooling afterwards help. Gentle massage towards the nipple can help; firm kneading is not advisable. With a fever above 38.5 degrees, chills or feeling very ill, you may have mastitis. Then please see a doctor. You can usually continue breastfeeding.

## Low milk supply?

Almost all women can produce enough milk. The feeling of having too little milk often comes from soft breasts or the baby’s restless behaviour, which is normal. A reliable sign is wet nappies (from day 5 at least five to six) and steady weight gain. What helps: feeding often, at least eight times in 24 hours in the first weeks, including at night, paying attention to a good latch, skin contact and rest. If your baby still isn’t gaining enough weight, talk to your midwife or paediatrician.

## Too much milk

A strong let-down reflex can make your baby choke. Breastfeeding lying down or leaning back helps, as does briefly taking the baby off during the first rush.

## Thrush

Whitish patches in the baby’s mouth and burning nipples can indicate thrush. Have it treated, usually in both mother and baby.

## Getting help

Midwives, lactation consultants (IBCLC), breastfeeding groups and La Leche League help. You don’t have to manage on your own.

Ultraschall arbeitet mit Schallwellen. S:
Ultrasound works with sound waves. They are reflected back and a computer turns them into an image. Unlike X-rays, no radiation is produced. During pregnancy, it is part of normal antenatal care.

## Three basic scans

According to the German maternity guidelines, three ultrasound scans are planned and paid for by your health insurer:

- from 8+0 to 11+6, that is weeks 9 to 12
- from 18+0 to 21+6, that is weeks 19 to 22
- from 28+0 to 31+6, that is weeks 29 to 32

Each has a different focus: the first is about where the pregnancy is located, the heartbeat, the number of babies and the due date. The second looks at growth, amniotic fluid, the position of the placenta and overall development. At the third, your doctor checks the baby’s growth and position.

## Further tests

If there is a medical reason, additional scans are possible, for example with bleeding, suspected growth problems or twins. These are also paid for by your health insurer. Options without a medical reason, such as a detailed anomaly scan without risk factors or first-trimester screening, are usually paid for yourself. Get advice on what they offer and what a result can mean.

## How safe is ultrasound?

When used correctly, ultrasound in antenatal care is considered safe. Still, it should only be used for a medical reason and only for as long as necessary. Purely “baby TV” appointments without a reason have not been allowed in Germany since 2021.

## What you can do

Ask what the doctor is measuring and what you are seeing. You can decide whether you want to know the sex or certain results. If you are unsure, counselling helps, including at a pregnancy advice centre.

Ultraschall ist ein Verfahren mit Schall:
Ultrasound uses sound waves and doesn’t involve X-rays. Statutory antenatal care in Germany includes three basic scans. If there are particular questions or risks, more are added.

## First scan: weeks 9 to 12

This is about whether the pregnancy is in the right place and intact, whether a heartbeat can be seen, how many babies there are and how big the baby is. The due date can be refined using the crown–rump length.

## Second scan: weeks 19 to 22

Now the baby is looked at from head to toe: growth, position of the organs, amount of amniotic fluid and position of the placenta. It is not a complete anomaly scan, but it can give indications. The sex can usually be seen, if you want to know.

## Third scan: weeks 29 to 32

It checks growth, the baby’s position, the amount of amniotic fluid and the placenta. Any abnormalities may be looked at more closely with a Doppler scan.

## Additional tests

- **First-trimester screening** (weeks 11 to 14): nuchal translucency and a blood test; it calculates a risk for certain chromosomal changes. Usually paid for yourself.
- **Detailed anomaly scan:** a detailed ultrasound by specialists, if there are risks or on request.
- **Doppler ultrasound:** shows the blood flow, for example if growth is delayed.

## Important to know

Ultrasound shows a lot, but not everything. A normal result is no guarantee, and an abnormal result is not a diagnosis. You have the right to be advised beforehand about the possibilities and limits, and also to decline certain tests. Ultrasound scans without a medical reason, such as 3D images just to look at, are not recommended.

Many mothers experience the “baby blues” in the first days after the birth: they are tearful, sensitive and exhausted. This is very common, usually starts two to five days after the birth, is linked to the hormonal changes and usually passes within two weeks.

## What helps with the baby blues

- Sleep as often as you can, including during the day
- Accept help with the housework and limit visitors
- Talk about it – with your partner, friends or your midwife
- Your midwife visits you at home in the first twelve weeks after the birth; in Germany, health insurance pays for this

## When it may be more

About ten to fifteen in a hundred mothers develop postnatal depression. It can begin in the first weeks, but also months after the birth. Signs can include:

- Persistent low mood lasting longer than two weeks
- No joy, not even in the baby
- Strong anxiety or feelings of guilt
- The feeling of not being a good mother or not being able to cope
- Sleep problems, even when the baby is sleeping
- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

Fathers and partners can also develop depression after the birth.

## Help is possible

Postnatal depression is very treatable, and it is nobody’s fault. Talk to your midwife, gynaecologist or GP. Often a short questionnaire already helps to assess the situation. Treatment includes talking, psychotherapy and sometimes medication. Many of these are compatible with breastfeeding. The Embryotox advisory service at the Charité can tell you whether a medicine is suitable. Some hospitals admit mother and baby together.

The association Schatten & Licht also provides help and contacts. Under “Find help” in Babyliebe there are further places to turn to. You’ll find more on anxiety, distressing thoughts and the rare postpartum psychosis in the guide “Anxiety, distressing thoughts and psychosis after the birth”.

## For partners and family

Take changes seriously and raise them kindly. Take over nights so she can sleep, and help to make an appointment. If you are worried, you can call the midwife or doctor yourself.

## In an acute crisis

Telefonseelsorge 0800 111 0 111 (free, around the clock) or emergency number 112. If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, call 112 immediately.

What you can see on ultrasound depends on the week, the baby’s position and the type of scan. The following details are guide values. Individual babies may be visible earlier or later.

## First trimester

- **From about week 5:** the gestational sac can be seen as a dark circle in the womb.
- **From about week 6:** a small embryo and the heart activity. It flickers like a dot.
- **About weeks 8 to 9:** head and body can be told apart, arm and leg buds are visible, and the baby moves.
- **About weeks 11 to 13:** the face in profile, hands, feet and the nuchal fold can be assessed.

## Second trimester

- **About weeks 14 to 16:** the sex may be visible if the baby is lying favourably.
- **About weeks 19 to 22:** the face, spine, heart chambers, stomach and kidneys can be roughly looked at in the basic scan. You can often see your baby swallowing or sucking their thumb.

## Third trimester

- **About weeks 29 to 32:** growth, amniotic fluid and position are the focus. The baby fills the space, and the face is often harder to see.
- **From week 36:** the head, belly and legs are so big that only parts fit in the picture. It’s normal not to be able to see much at once any more.

## Black, grey, white

Fluids such as amniotic fluid appear black, bones bright white and soft tissue grey. That’s why bones and amniotic fluid are easy to see, while the face only appears as a soft outline.

Weinen ist das wichtigste Kommunikations: Crying is a baby’s most important means of communication: hunger, tiredness, a full nappy, the need for closeness, overstimulation or tummy ache. Weinen ist die Sprache deines Babys. Es:
Crying is your baby’s language. It says: I’m hungry, I’m tired, I’m too warm or too cold, I need you. Some babies cry a lot without anything being wrong. This is exhausting and stressful, but it passes.

## What’s normal?

In the first three months of life, babies cry on average two to three hours a day. It increases until week 6 and usually decreases afterwards. A baby is considered to cry excessively if they cry for more than three hours a day on at least three days a week for more than three weeks (the rule of three). The cause is usually unclear; wind and overstimulation are discussed. Colic usually ends around the fourth month.

## What you can try

- Check needs: hunger, nappy, temperature, tiredness, closeness
- Carrying, cradling, rocking, singing or talking calmly
- Reduce stimulation: dimmed light, a quiet room, fewer visitors
- The “tiger in the tree” hold, warm hands on the belly, a clockwise tummy massage
- Walks or a car ride
- Steady sounds such as a vacuum cleaner or white noise

Not everything helps every time. It’s not a failure if your baby keeps crying.

## When to see a doctor?

If there is fever, vomiting, blood in the stool, a bloated hard belly, poor feeding, or if you feel something isn’t right, have your baby examined.

## When you reach your limits

Constant crying wears anyone down. If you feel angry or desperate, put your baby down safely in their cot, go to another room and take a breath. Call someone. **Never shake:** shaking can cause severe brain damage.

Help is available around the clock:

- Elterntelefon, parents’ helpline (Nummer gegen Kummer): 0800 111 0 550
- Telefonseelsorge: 0800 111 0 111
- Clinics for excessively crying babies (Schreibabyambulanzen) and Frühe Hilfen: reachable via the youth welfare office or your midwife
- Out-of-hours medical service: 116 117, emergency number: 112

Asking for help is a strength. Share the nights, accept support and allow yourself breaks.

Wie du mit Wehenschmerzen umgehst, entsc:
How you deal with labour pain is your decision – even spontaneously during the birth. There is no right or wrong.

## Without medication

- Breathing, making sounds, changing position and moving
- Warmth, massage, counter-pressure on the sacrum
- The birthing pool or a shower
- A familiar birth partner and a calm environment

## With medication

- Gas and air (nitrous oxide): short-acting; you control it yourself through a mask. Not available in all hospitals.
- Painkillers by injection or drip
- Epidural: very effective numbing through a catheter in your back. You are awake and can usually keep working with your body.

Write your wishes down in your birth plan and discuss them in advance when you register at the hospital.

## More about the epidural

An epidural relieves pain very well for most women. It can lengthen the pushing stage, and assistance with a ventouse or forceps is needed more often. Some women get low blood pressure or itching. Whether and when it is possible is clarified with you by the anaesthetics team. Many hospitals offer the information session before the birth.

You may change your mind at any time, even if you had planned something different beforehand.

Write in your birth plan what you would like and what you would rather not have. This helps the team even if you don’t feel like talking much at the time.

In addition to the basic scans, there are prenatal diagnostic options. You decide for yourself whether you want to use them. A “no” is just as fine as a “yes”.

## First-trimester screening

Between 11+0 and 13+6, the doctor measures the nuchal translucency on ultrasound and combines it with a blood test. From this, a probability for certain chromosomal conditions is calculated. The result is not a diagnosis. You usually pay for it yourself.

## Non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT)

It examines the baby’s genetic material in the mother’s blood, from week 10. Since July 2022, health insurers in Germany pay for it in justified individual cases after medical counselling. It too provides a probability. If the result is abnormal, it is clarified by a further test.

## Detailed anomaly scan

A detailed organ scan by specialists, usually in weeks 20 to 22. Health insurance pays for it if there is a medical reason. Without a reason, you pay for it yourself.

## What an abnormal result means

An abnormal finding doesn’t mean your baby is ill. It is a reason for a counselling appointment and often for further tests. You are entitled to medical counselling before and after every test and to psychosocial counselling, for example at pregnancy advice centres. This counselling is free.

## Before you decide

Think beforehand about what you would do with a result, and talk to your doctor or midwife about it. Take your time; you don’t have to agree straight away.
Zusätzlich zu jodiertem Salz, Milchprodu: In addition to iodised salt, dairy products and sea fish, during pregnancy and breastfeeding. If you have a thyroid condition, check with your doctor first.
Zuverlässig ab dem Tag, an dem deine Per: Reliably from the day your period is due. Some tests show something earlier, but are less reliable then. It’s best to test with your first morning urine. A positive test should be confirmed by a gynaecologist.

Zwei Tagesschläfchen werden zu ein bis z: Two daytime naps become one to two. Many children don’t sleep through the night yet; that’s normal.
Zwei- bis dreimal pro Woche reicht, häuf: Two to three times a week is enough; bathing more often dries out the skin. The water should be about 37 degrees; a bath thermometer helps. Never leave your baby alone, not even for a moment. Bath briefly (5 to 10 minutes) and then dry well, especially in skin folds.

Zwillinge kommen im Durchschnitt früher:
On average, twins arrive earlier than single babies, usually around weeks 36 to 37. For uncomplicated twins, a birth between weeks 36 and 38 is often planned. Monochorionic twins tend to be born a little earlier. The team decides together with you when and how.

## Where?

Choose a hospital that has experience with twin births and a children’s hospital nearby, ideally a perinatal centre. Discuss this in good time so that you don’t have to find your way around anew in an emergency.

## How?

A vaginal birth is often possible if the first baby is head down and the pregnancy has gone without complications. Studies show no advantage of a planned caesarean in this situation. If the first baby is lying differently or there are risks, a caesarean is often recommended. Once the first baby is born, the second often arrives within about an hour.

## What’s different

- More professionals are in the room, often a second doctor and paediatricians too.
- An IV line and continuous monitoring of both heartbeats are usual.
- The babies may go to the children’s hospital for observation afterwards, even if they are doing well.

## Preparation

- Talk about your wishes during pregnancy and write them in your birth plan.
- Pack your hospital bag earlier, from about week 30.
- Plan help for the time afterwards and clarify questions about maternity protection (twelve weeks after the birth) and parental allowance (multiple-birth supplement).

If you have bleeding, leaking amniotic fluid or contractions before week 37, go to the hospital immediately.

As a guide, the British guideline gives about every two weeks from week 16 for monochorionic twins and about every four weeks from week 20 for dichorionic twins. Your practice or hospital sets the exact plan.

Übelkeit beginnt meist um die 6. SSW und:
Nausea usually starts around week 6 and eases noticeably for most between weeks 12 and 16. It’s unpleasant, but a normal sign of the hormonal changes.

## What helps many people

- Eat something dry in the morning before getting up, for example a rusk
- Several small meals instead of three large ones
- Drinks between meals, in small sips
- Avoid strong smells, get plenty of fresh air
- Ginger in tea or food
- Enough rest – tiredness makes nausea worse

## When you need medical help

If you vomit several times a day, can hardly keep anything down, lose weight or pass very little urine, you may have hyperemesis gravidarum. Then please see your doctor promptly – there are well-tolerated medicines and drips.

## Medication

There are medicines for severe nausea that have been well studied in pregnancy. Get medical advice about them. The Embryotox advisory service of the Charité gives independent information. Don’t take anything just because it’s herbal.

## In everyday life

Talk to your employer if you need breaks. Don’t brush your teeth straight after vomiting; rinse your mouth with water first. This protects your tooth enamel.

Some people find an acupressure wristband helpful. It can’t do any harm, but a reliable effect has not been proven.
